articles.description: The transition to electric vehicles should be moving apace, but it is not. And why? Incompetence, expedience and cowardice This is how it works. An industry puts tremendous effort into resisting change: lobbying governments, mobilising the media, pouring money into junktanks . It argues that a transition would threaten jobs, or damage the national interest, or harm poor people, while what it really fears is the cost of retooling its plants or developing new protocols. Then, when the inevitable cliff edge approaches, it whines that change is coming too soon. For reasons beyond its control, it isn’t ready, so the government must delay its plans. This is what triggered the Dutch nitrate crisis , and the UK’s repeated “emergency” exemptions from the ban on a devastating class of pesticides. Now the same dynamic is driving the UK’s crisis over the transition to electric vehicles (EVs). The result is that, as the global climate summit, Cop31 , begins, it looks as if our gift to the world will be a major, predictable and entirely avoidable increase in the UK’s greenhouse gas emissions. articles.description: Even her own MPs were stony-faced as the Tory leader ran though her set list of gags from the budget to Russell Brand UK politics live – latest updates Well, there was one person at least who thought Kemi Badenoch had absolutely nailed it at this week’s prime minister’s questions. And that person was Kemi Badenoch. She could not have been more pleased with herself if she had tried. No one laughed louder and longer at her own jokes than she did. No one admired her laser focus as much as she did. Kemi is the paid up chief executive of her own fanclub. As for the rest of her Tory MPs – aside from Chris Philp, who is basically a parasitic homunculus – they weren’t quite so convinced by Kemi’s performance. She had been so entranced with her one-liners, she had forgotten to ask any serious questions. And never forget how low the gag bar is in the Commons. What passes as a joke at PMQs wouldn’t even register as humour in normal conversation. Wouldn’t even elicit the groan that comes from the recognition of a gag format. Continue reading...

articles.title: KKR and RWE are rich firms. Why do they need a UK state loan for their windfarms? | Nils Pratley
articles.description: National wealth fund is to lend £1bn towards the Vanguard projects – but whether the private equity giant needed help is debatable “This major investment in UK renewables is a vote of confidence for building in Britain,” declared the prime minister. Andy Burnham is obviously correct that the two Vanguard windfarms off the coast of Norfolk are huge investments . Together, they require almost £13bn of debt financing. But he can’t claim they represent a fresh expression of confidence. The project has been on the runway since the German utility RWE, the developer, was awarded a contract to build the windfarms in January’s renewables auction. Continue reading...

articles.title: Chickens are synonymous with cowardice. Is it time to stick up for our feathered friends? | Adrian Chiles
articles.description: After Peta’s call ‘to reject mischaracterisations of chickens’, I wonder what they would make of Polish representations of polecats and Croatian cuckoos Chickens don’t have it easy. On top of living largely crap, short lives, they endure the ignominy of collectively being a byword for cowardice. The campaign group People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (Peta) has written to the Oxford English Dictionary asking for this definition of “chicken” to be changed. Naturally enough, there are those who have been unafraid to holler “Woke nonsense!” as loud as cocks crowing. For my part, I think Peta is right to stick up for chickens, but I’m not sure removing a definition – assuming definition-removal is a thing – would make any difference. Chicken, in this sense, is in common use as an adjective, a verb and a noun. It’s got deep roots that are going to take some shifting. And any such move could open up a right can of worms (sorry, worms). What about the vulture, rat, shark and sloth lobbies? Not to mention pigs, snakes, weasels, donkeys, sheep, dogs, parrots and all manner of creatures with whom we share this beleaguered planet. Continue reading...

articles.title: It’s impeachment season! After the attempt on Pete Hegseth, will Donald Trump be next? | Arwa Mahdawi
articles.description: Trump has already made history as the only president to be impeached twice. After the Republicans’ thrashing in the midterms, could there be a third attempt? The days are getting shorter, the nights are getting longer and some Republicans are getting nervous. After a long stretch of impunity, it’s impeachment season in the US. While the attempt to impeach the defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, failed yesterday , Donald Trump may be worried he’s next. In January, the president warned Republicans that they had better win the November elections or he would be in big trouble. “If we don’t win the midterms … they’ll find a reason to impeach me,” Trump said . He repeated this plea to voters during an October rally in Oklahoma : “Pretend I’m running, please. Just pretend. ’Cause I am on the ballot. And if we don’t win, they’ll end up impeaching me.” Continue reading...

articles.title: From blood group ID to cycle racks: I asked for little ways to fix broken Britain and the public’s ideas give me hope | Martin Lewis
articles.description: There are thousands of small tips to make our country better. People know what is wrong, and it’s clear they have solutions Have you ever come across an annoying little problem and thought, “why don’t they just fix that?” If so, I want to hear from you. I’m looking for your ideas for practical, low-cost, non-controversial ways to improve the UK – whether that’s health, schools, transport, business, housing, policing, justice, tech, shopping, money – or owt else entirely. The spark for this happened just over a year ago, when I spoke at Politico’s fringe event at Labour’s conference. The key discussion was about Keir Starmer’s unpopularity. I was asked what I’d have advised the government when it took power, so I said : “Come up with 100 small things that piss people off and that you can fix, and they can see that you have fixed them.” Then I reeled off a list of small fixes for my subject area: the counterproductive way council tax debt is escalated; renaming “tax-free childcare”; and so on. Tell people their blood group at their first adult blood test. Knowing you’ve a common or rare type may make you more inclined to donate. It’s a brilliantly simple nudge that could widen the do

articles.title: The Guardian view on Maga after the midterms: doubling down on Trumpism | Editorial
articles.description: Republicans know that the president’s folly and excesses cost them the elections. That doesn’t mean they’re ready to challenge him Shortly after polls closed last Tuesday, with the scale of the Republican trouncing in the midterms still becoming apparent, Donald Trump briefly adopted an oddly conciliatory tone. He declared that he was “absolutely” willing to accept the results, would look forward to working with Democrats and that deportation policies might have been “ too tough ”. It was never going to last. He soon cast doubt on the elections’ legitimacy. On Friday, he replaced his chief of staff, Susie Wiles, with her deputy, Stephen Miller – a white nationalist, or “stone-cold racist”, in the words of Hakeem Jeffries, likely to be the next House speaker. Ms Wiles executed the president’s decisions faithfully, but was seen as a somewhat calming if not restraining influence, which may help explain her departure. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Guardian view on welfare reform: time to retire lazy myths and stereotypes | Editorial
articles.description: A speech by the leader of the opposition exemplifies much that is wrong with the way British politics conventionally talks about benefit claimants There is a big difference between expenditure that is rising and a rise that is “out of control”. The amount Britain spends on social security is in the former category. Too much political rhetoric around the subject assumes that it is in the latter one. The Office for Budget Responsibility forecasts the growth in welfare spending over the next five years at 0.2%-0.5% of gross domestic product, from £353bn this year to £431bn in 2032. That money might well be suboptimally deployed. There are rival demands on the state’s resources and a reasonable debate to be had about priorities at the Department for Work and Pensions. But that is not the tone of the debate routinely conducted in Westminster. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in our letters section, please click here . Continue reading...

articles.title: Russell Brand’s trial, rape myths and a questionable faith | Letters
articles.description: Readers respond to reporting on the disgraced actor and comedian’s trial and conviction for rape and sexual assault You report that in the wake of Russell Brand’s trial, the government pledged “to examine calls to crack down on ‘rape myths’ in trials” ( Russell Brand suspected to have attacked at least 10 other women, 6 November ). This is not the first time the treatment of women in trials for rape, and the perpetuation of rape myths, has been drawn to the attention of a Labour government. Sue Lees (1941-2002), a former colleague from the Polytechnic/University of North London conducted research into the reporting of rape in the media and how it was treated within the English legal system in the 1990s. Continue reading...

articles.title: Hacked fridges and other dangers lurking in the ‘internet of shit’ | Letters
articles.description: One reader sounds a warning about all our devices that are connected to the internet, following a series of cyber-attacks on supermarket fridges Well done to Alex Pearce for unplugging his fridge from the internet ( Hot fridges, a fake nuclear alert and a $6bn heist: are we in the foothills of a hacking epidemic?, 8 November ). My only question is why he didn’t do it a few weeks earlier, when the first round of hacked fridges were headline news for several days. Your article notes that there are millions of devices connected to the internet. This sea of domestic and industrial controllers, known as the “internet of things” in marketing literature and the “internet of shit” by engineers, all have several things in common: their firmware is almost never upgraded, software security features are a fig leaf and the vast majority can run without an internet connection. Continue reading...

articles.title: Clearing up confusion over iodine in milk | Letters
articles.description: Cow’s milk is not a natural source of iodine. It is fortified, at the cow, notes Dale Vince of the Green Britain Foundation You report that scientists say moving even partly from dairy products to vegan alternatives could lead to deficiencies in iodine and other micronutrients if the substitutes are not fortified ( Swapping from dairy to plant-based milk, cheese and yoghurt ‘could lead to micronutrient deficiencies’, 4 November ). To be clear, cow’s milk is not a natural source of iodine. It is fortified, at the cow. As the paper published in the Lancet Planetary Health explains, iodine is in milk because it is added to cattle feed. The vitamin B12 is there because cobalt is added to the feed so the cow’s gut bacteria can make it. Britain has been doing this for decades. If fortification is the answer, and the paper’s authors say it is, then fortify plant milk. It’s better for us and the planet than cow’s milk. Continue reading...

articles.title: Asylum law changes are causing refugee families like mine terrible worry | Letter
articles.description: A reader highlights how the government’s immigration changes are affecting those who have been granted asylum and wish to apply for indefinite leave to remain I am writing as a refugee who has lived in the UK since 2007. I claimed asylum in 2007, and my appeal was allowed by the first-tier tribunal (immigration and asylum) in February 2020. However, because of Home Office delays, I did not receive my five-year refugee permission until June 2022. I applied for indefinite leave to remain in June 2025, but my application was refused because I had not completed five years from the date my refugee permission was granted. I was therefore expecting to apply again in June 2027. Continue reading...

articles.title: Meeting of two lost souls: can Pochettino make it work at Manchester United? | Barney Ronay
articles.description: Manager has been hurt by experiences at elite clubs but several players at Old Trafford could fit his playing style Welcome, Mauricio, to the meat grinder. Or rather, welcome back. We’ve been expecting you. There is nothing surprising in the news Manchester United may be on the verge of appointing Mauricio Pochettino. United are always on the verge of appointing Pochettino. This is a club that has spent 13 years hiring and firing the same structurally doomed manager – same shellshocked eyes, same irresolvable macro-problems – and the last eight years almost but not quite doing this to Pochettino. Well, maybe we’re finally here. Maybe he just needed to be broken enough to make it fit. And who knows, perhaps there is even a kind of accidental synergy here. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘I’ve had to prove people wrong’: Kane still striving before record England cap
articles.description: Captain to surpass Shilton with 126th cap against Croatia Kane aims to increase record for younger players to catch Harry Kane says he still feels a pressure to prove his worth, even as he prepares to become England’s most capped men’s player, as he outlined his determination to set records that will stand for years. The captain will make his 126th appearance against Croatia at ­Wembley on Thursday night, moving him ahead of Peter Shilton on the all-time list. Kane is England’s record ­goalscorer with 91, comfortably clear of Wayne Rooney, who retired with 53. Continue reading...

articles.title: England return to site of Ashes angst but Australia gaze stuck on sandpaper
articles.description: White-ball tour begins in Perth on Friday but there is only one story in Australian cricket and the tourists are not it It feels like five minutes since England were last in pristine Perth, preparing – or rather under-preparing – to win back the Ashes, only for their glass jaw to be shattered by the flashing blade of Travis Head and a two-day defeat at Optus Stadium . But 12 months on, the mood is much changed. Beyond the fact this is merely a white-ball tour – three one-day internationals starting on Friday, followed by five Twenty20s – England’s main character energy has seemingly evaporated. Brendon McCullum is still the head coach in limited-overs cricket but no one is talking about “Bazball” or trying to sell it as some kind of sequel. Continue reading...

articles.title: Complaint filed to IRS in relation to Fifa head Gianni Infantino’s housekeeper
articles.description: It calls for inquiry into claims she was on Fifa payroll Fifa: Infantino personally pays for ‘any domestic staff’ A complaint has been filed to the United States Internal Revenue Service calling for an investigation into claims an individual on the Fifa payroll was working privately as a housekeeper for Gianni Infantino. If the IRS investigates and finds the claims to be proven then Fifa could lose its tax-exempt status in the US. Fifa has 501(c)(4) status in the country, a category for organisations “created to promote community welfare for charitable, educational or recreational purposes”. Continue reading...

articles.title: Jockey Tom O’Brien, Cheltenham festival winner, dies aged 39
articles.description: O’Brien rode more than 1,000 winners over jumps ‘Tom meant so much to so many people across our sport’ Tom O’Brien, who rode more than 1,000 winners over jumps including five Grade Ones and two at the Cheltenham festival, has died at the age of 39 after being diagnosed with cancer. O’Brien, who retired from race riding in April 2023, had a close association with Philip Hobbs’s stable near Minehead throughout his 20-year career in the saddle and enjoyed his most prestigious Grade One victories aboard Hobbs’s Thyme Hill in the Stayers’ Hurdle at Aintree in April 2021 and the Kauto Star Novice Chase at Kempton in December 2022. Continue reading...

articles.title: Danny Kelly, football broadcaster and renowned editor, dies aged 69
articles.description: Danny Baker pays tribute to the ‘funniest man I knew’ Kelly was former editor of the NME and Q magazines The journalist and broadcaster Danny Kelly, who helped define coverage of music and football in the UK for a generation, has died at the age of 69. Kelly edited the NME and Q magazine, and launched the Football 365 website before going on to be a presenter and pundit on the BBC and TalkSport. He had been receiving treatment for oesophageal cancer. Continue reading...

articles.title: Eddie Jones retains his passion and divisive power heading into England reunion
articles.description: Japan head coach was criticised for discarding players harshly during his Red Rose tenure but that tough love has paid off for some To listen to Eddie Jones chewing the fat on assorted podcasts this week is to admire the enduring thickness of his coaching skin. The old crocodile smile is still intact too, along with his sense of humour after an interaction in a lift with a fan after his Japan side’s 28-21 weekend defeat in Cardiff . As Jones later confided: “This Welsh bloke came up to me and said: ‘You almost look human with your glasses on.’” Next up is a reunion with a few former friends – and foes – at Twickenham. While it is now almost four years since Jones was sacked by the Rugby Football Union , there remain mixed emotions on both sides. Those relieved to see him go in late 2022 will certainly not be too brokenhearted if there is a similar outcome to the last time a Jones-coached Japan came to Allianz Stadium two years ago and lost 59-14 . Continue reading...

articles.title: Svitolina stays in WTA Finals hunt after remarkable fightback sees off Muchova
articles.description: Ukrainian wins 3-6, 6-2, 6-2 after eight-minute timeout Andreeva beats Sabalenka 6-4, 6-0 to top Group B Elina Svitolina staged a remarkable comeback to beat Karolina Muchova and remain in the hunt for the WTA Finals title. But she recovered to win 3-6, 6-2, 6-2 and stay in with a chance of reaching the semi-finals. Continue reading...

articles.title: Stephen Curry attacks treatment of women after former players criticize wife Ayesha’s movie kiss
articles.description: Warriors star defends wife over romantic comedy role Arenas called Ayesha ‘only blemish’ on Curry family Four-time NBA champion condemns double standards Golden State Warriors star Stephen Curry has criticized several ex-professional athletes for questioning his wife Ayesha’s decision to appear in a romantic comedy featuring an on-screen kiss, accusing them of diminishing her accomplishments and perpetuating double standards about women. The four-time NBA champion posted a 90-second video on Instagram on Wednesday in response to comments by former NBA players Gilbert Arenas and Nick Young, as well as former NFL players Emmanuel Acho and LeSean McCoy, following the release of Ayesha Curry’s new film, Second Chance Holiday. articles.description: PM wrote to transport commissioner to oppose ‘megashed’ in Astley shortly before he entered No 10 Andy Burnham raised safety concerns about dozens of lorries leaving a “monster” warehouse near a primary school because there was “no safe crossing” for children, a public inquiry has heard. articles.title: Hoax bomb threats made to schools in Scotland, Northern Ireland and Italy
articles.description: Police assure parents and teachers there is no danger as thousands of schools in Italy and hundreds in the UK affected Hundreds of schools in Scotland and Northern Ireland were hit by a fresh wave of hoax bomb threats on Wednesday, with some sites evacuated as a precaution. Police in Scotland said that about 1,000 schools, from Dumfries in the south of Scotland to Aberdeenshire and Orkney in the north, had received the hoax warnings. At least 300 schools were affected in Northern Ireland. Similar claims were sent in a “generic communication” to schools in the Republic of Ireland. Continue reading...

articles.title: Two skulls likely belonging to enslaved people returned to Brazil after Harvard used them in eugenics studies
articles.description: Remains believed to have belonged to Africans or Afro-Brazilians repatriated after being flown back by diplomats Two skulls, including that of a man believed to have taken part in Brazil’s greatest slave revolt but whose remains were taken to the United States and used in racist eugenics studies at Harvard University, were repatriated on Wednesday. The remains had been outside Brazil since the 19th century. One was taken about 190 years ago from Salvador, the capital of the state of Bahia; the other, about 160 years ago, from Rio de Janeiro – and were welcomed back in moving, subdued ceremonies in both cities. Continue reading...

articles.title: Argentinian lawyer mocks UK’s sovereignty claim in Falklands oil case

Marcelo Kohen, representing Argentina at a hearing in Hamburg, mocked Britain for apparently believing in the historic doctrine that the British crown has sovereignty over expansive parts of the oceans. articles.title: Bird flu fears prompt orders for farmers to keep poultry inside in England and Scotland
articles.description: Increased risk of devastating strain means restrictions imposed for second year in a row on those keeping birds Poultry and captive birds across England and Scotland must be kept inside for the second year in a row due to an increased risk of a devastating strain of bird flu. The British government has issued an England-wide avian influenza prevention zone, meaning individuals with 50 or more poultry or captive birds must house them inside. articles.title: Bird flu has caused catastrophic die-offs – could a wave of extinctions follow?
articles.description: As the IUCN global conservation body prepares to update its red list of endangered species, scientists explain why calculating the true toll of a pandemic is so hard It began with the brown skuas. The migratory seabirds had arrived on the sub-Antarctic island of South Georgia in 2023, harbouring a deadly passenger. Within months, the southern elephant seals that had come ashore to breed became sick. Mothers and newborn pups were weak and trembling, with many struggling to breathe. What followed was a horrific mass casualty event, caused by the highly infectious avian influenza (H5N1). By 2025, more than 53,000 female elephant seals had died on South Georgia. That is especially alarming, scientists say, because the island is home to more than half of the global breeding population . Continue reading...

articles.title: Thousands without shelter face lethal conditions in storm-hit Gaza as they wait for 150,000 tents
articles.description: Charities warn of lack of protection amid health fears for more than 940,000 displaced people living in flood-prone areas Tens of thousands of Palestinians have been left in waterlogged and damaged tents after deadly storms at the weekend, while 150,000 new shelters are held outside Gaza awaiting Israeli approval to enter, aid agencies have said. articles.title: Thousands of rare wildflowers rescued from eroding Scottish coast

articles.title: Labour MPs warn against weakening electric vehicle targets ahead of crunch talks

articles.title: Morgan McSweeney calls for rethink of UK cabinet ministers’ ‘quasi-judicial’ powers

articles.title: BMI alternative for identifying obesity ‘could prevent misdiagnosis in millions’
articles.description: Combining body mass index with other measurements and tests would lead to better care and outcomes, experts say An alternative to BMI for diagnosing obesity could prevent misdiagnosis in millions of people worldwide, according to doctors who found it more accurately distinguished healthy people from those with harmful excess body fat. Medical experts have long considered body mass index a blunt instrument for defining obesity, leading to concerns that substantial numbers of people with excess body fat are missed while others who are healthy are wrongly diagnosed. articles.title: Diesel still costing close to a ‘dismal’ £2 a litre despite oil price falls
articles.description: Pump prices stay stubbornly high as leading bank official warns energy costs are likely to remain ‘elevated’ The price of diesel on UK forecourts remains stubbornly close to October’s record high of £2 despite a sharp fall in oil prices. articles.title: Nvidia hires leading US law firm to investigate Jensen Huang’s relationship

articles.title: Nissan reduces petrol car production as EV sales boom in China

articles.title: Prime property, slow sales: why London’s stock of empty high-end flats is piling up

There are ultra-modern blocks in the most upmarket neighbourhoods – including Chelsea, Kensington and Mayfair – that offer marble lobbies, concierge services and views across the city’s skyline. The problem for property developers is finding wealthy residents to fill them , leaving brand-new properties in London’s most desirable postcodes standing empty. Continue reading...

articles.title: Does M John Harrison’s Booker win mean science fiction is finally accepted by a ‘snobby’ literary establishment?
articles.description: Kazuo Ishiguro, Jeff VanderMeer, Olivia Laing and other writers weigh in on the publishing world’s genre wars As M John Harrison was announced as the Booker prize winner on Monday evening, the 81-year-old looked gobsmacked. Decades into his career, and long overlooked by the mainstream literary establishment, he had just won a prize that has never before rewarded a writer known for science fiction, with a decidedly fantastical book. His fans, many leading authors among them, are thrilled. “For decades it was a standard – and correct – nerd whine to point out that sentence for sentence, book for book, Harrison was one of the greatest writers out there, full stop, but that ‘mainstream’ prizes never reflected that,” says China Miéville, who last week won the Goldsmiths prize with his 1,200-page speculative novel The Rouse . Back in 2002, Miéville wrote that Harrison not having won a Booker by that point proved “the bankruptcy and back-slapping generic snobbery of the literary establishment”. Now, he says: “I am so delighted, for Harrison, and for fiction.” Continue reading...

articles.title: How to Rob a Bank review – Amazon’s anti-capitalist caper is far from a riot
articles.description: Nicholas Hoult, Anna Sawai and Pete Davidson play Robin Hood in this simple-minded and unexciting attempt to mix social commentary with action In case you were somehow blissfully unaware, America is in a very dark place and Americans are not very happy about it. Last week’s midterms saw a historic blue wave propelled by the high cost of living and the low trust in those making decisions, but restoring any small shred of faith in the system and any vague semblance of financial equity is still unlikely to come anytime soon. It’s therefore theoretically ideal timing for films that provide some sort of rousing David v Goliath catharsis, a win on-screen when one feels entirely out of reach in real life. But like Paul Greengrass’s muddy and muddled peasant revolt drama The Uprising which crashed and burned in September, David Leitch’s How to Rob a Bank can’t quite find a way to capture a moment that should be easy to capture. The director is best known for synthetic action films that prioritise noise above all else, from Deadpool 2 to Bullet Train to Hobbs & Shaw, a tonal throughline that could be most generously described as “annoying”. Continue reading...

articles.title: Rivals review – this TV joy is so much more than just a romp
articles.description: It’s not just backcombing, betrayals and bonking in this second part of series two. There are moments of real poignancy Tony Baddingham? Tony Worse-ingham, more like! For reasons best known, one suspects, to streaming giant Disney’s revenue-maximisers, the second series of Rivals has been split up into two parts of six episodes each. We left the rutting folk of Rutshire just after Rupert Campbell-Black (Alex Hassell, a sex god by way of Hugh Laurie and once you notice this you can’t unsee it) had broken the news to arch-rival Tony (David Tennant, having the time of his life as the unrepentantly villainous mogul) that his wife, Monica (Claire Rushbrook), had been killed. She drove off into the Great Storm of 1987 after discovering Tony’s affair with Maud (Victoria Smurfit), his bitter enemy’s wife, and demanding – at last – a divorce. One tree later, however, poor Monica’s dreams of freedom and future happiness ended. Now, after a five-month hiatus for viewers, we arrive at the funeral. Never has there been more lustful inter-pew side-eyeing. Taggie (Bella Maclean, doing such fine work with what could be a tremendously boring character) and Rupert Reformed-Bounder-Question-Mark are

articles.title: Prima Facie review – Cynthia Erivo’s brilliant barrister blazes in sexual assault drama
articles.description: Adaptation of the international stage hit stars a commanding Erivo as Tessa, whose career defending rape suspects is undermined by experience A blazingly fierce, effortlessly commanding central performance from Cynthia Erivo, like something from classical drama, powers this movie adaptation of Suzie Miller’s international stage hit (which starred Sheridan Harbridge in the original Australian production , and then Jodie Comer in London’s West End ). Miller has written the screenplay, with Susanna White directing . In the theatre, it is a bravura solo spectacle, a stream-of-consciousness torrent which puts you right inside the trauma and the terror. The movie opens things out to a more conventionally presented drama and we lose something of that overwhelming moment-by-moment access to the lead character’s inner thoughts. But the resulting story is robustly constructed and tremendously acted. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power season three review – this dull show’s revamp is too little, too late
articles.description: They’ve sidelined the harfoots, introduced a Stranger Things star and thrown in full-blooded romance. It’s probably not enough to stop the fantasy prequel feeling boring, though It might seem strange to characterise the leading streaming show from one of the most dominant corporations on the planet as a scrappy underdog. But after a lavish-but-dramatically stilted debut in 2022 and a similarly well-heeled but darker second season in 2024 , it does feel like prequel series The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power is somehow stuck on the back foot. For all its finely wrought art direction and respect for JRR Tolkien’s elaborate high-fantasy taxonomy, this no-expense-spared expansion of the mythos – set in the Second Age of Middle-earth, thousands of years before Bilbo Baggins first went walkabout – is in danger of going down in our own historical annals as simply a bit dull. Never mind more rings, it desperately needs some rizz. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘My partners would all tell you I was a nut job’: Jane Wiedlin on the Go-Go’s, fame and the freedom of sex dungeons
articles.description: As she releases a brutally honest memoir, the new wave icon opens up about industry sexism, living with bipolar disorder and becoming ‘the world’s first atheist ordained minister’ The first thing Jane Wiedlin tells me before our interview even begins is that, an hour or so earlier, she downed two beers. “It keeps me cheerful,” she says with a laugh. The disclosure dovetails with the reason we’re doing the interview in the first place, which is to unpack her new memoir, a tome that deserves a truth-in-advertising award for its title alone: TMI (as in “too much information”). “I’ve always been TMI!” Wiedlin proudly announces. “I’m the one who always wanted to expose the truth. This book is my first opportunity to do so.” A portion of that truth has to do with the band she helped form in the late 70s, the Go-Go’s. The five-piece are not only the first all-female band who play their own instruments and write their own material to earn a No 1 album in the US but, astonishingly, are the only such group to hold that distinction nearly 45 years later. The group’s power-pop music, heard in zippy hits like Our Lips Are Sealed and Vacation, led to their induction into the Rock and Roll Hall o

articles.title: U2: Carnaval de Luz review – rousing, restorative rock from a band ready to take on the world again
articles.description: (Island) On their first album of new songs in nearly a decade, even earnest Bono-isms carry weight amid music that is impassioned and rejuvenated Even artists who enjoy a seemingly unstoppable imperial period eventually seem to encounter spells of turbulence when the creative planets no longer align – which has been the story of U2’s last 20 years. Try as they might, nothing has matched their earlier albums – especially that mostly uninterrupted golden run from their 1980 debut Boy to 90s benchmarks Achtung Baby and Zooropa. They’ve tried going more pop, becoming more experimental, touring 1987 colossus The Joshua Tree again and even reworking old songs for 2023’s Songs of Surrender, but nothing has uncorked the genie again, or given the band the kind of relevance they had for so many years. Often, it felt as though they were trying too hard. Continue reading...

articles.title: Chris Packham’s lovely new wildlife show: best podcasts of the week
articles.description: Nature fans can get nerdy questions answered in this weekly video pod. Plus, Siobhán McSweeney is your new Comfort Eating host! “Are bats really blind?” “What are wasps for?” These are the types of question Chris Packham and his team – Kyle Thomas and Megan McCubbin – want to answer for you in this lovely new video podcast (which also streams on Fridays at 7.30pm on BBC Two ). They give a weekly wildlife dispatch from their pod nestled in the countryside somewhere near Bristol, with guest experts and “guaranteed nerdiness”. Hollie Richardson BBC Sounds, episodes weekly Continue reading...

articles.title: Beethoven: Symphony No 3 album review – thrilling, but Minasi’s determination to shock often feels self-conscious
articles.description: Ensemble Resonanz/Minasi (Harmonia Mundi) Riccardo Minasi radically reassesses the Eroica, bringing its acerbic innovation to the fore in a startling and compelling new recording that will surely prompt heated debate In 1816, a young Franz Schubert took a swipe at Beethoven, accusing him of promoting a musical eccentricity that muddled “the agreeable with the repulsive, heroism with howlings and the holiest with harlequinades” in order to “goad people to madness”. In this colours-to-the-mast recording, Riccardo Minasi demonstrates precisely what contemporaries were afraid of with a radical reassessment of the Eroica Symphony. Looking to original sources, he strips away the modifications of centuries to lay the symphony before us in all its acerbic 19th-century innovation. The results are certainly startling. Antsy modern strings tear up the musical tarmac in the opening movement as period brass and percussion hammer nails into the coffin of Mozartian classicism. Dynamic markings are interpreted to the max as the funeral march shrieks and shudders, the scherzo gallops and the finale stamps its feet. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Homosexuality was coined by a Hungarian’: the gay-sauna travelogue questioning central Europe’s illiberal image
articles.description: A new book, With Wittgenstein in a Gay Sauna, reveals the deep-rooted queer subcultures in cities from Budapest to Prague – defying regional stereotypes and inspiring an art exhibition on masculinity The philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein argued that our understanding of reality is fundamentally bound by and shaped by the language we use to talk about it. But there is one place where the Vienna-born thinker’s argument ceases to make sense. “Gay saunas are spaces where language dies,” says Vratislav Maňák, a Czech writer and literary scholar. With Wittgenstein in a Gay Sauna, a book that made a major splash when it was published in Czech and German earlier this year, Maňák fictionalises Wittgenstein, who had romantic relations with both men and women , entering a Viennese Herrensauna called Kaiserbründl, hailed in newspapers at the time as “the most stylish bathing establishment in the world”. Continue reading...

articles.title: Ten Lives by Mona Chalabi review – what if we were totally honest about our wealth?
articles.description: The data journalist puts her own finances – and those of 10 others from across the economic spectrum – under a microscope How much do you earn? If the question makes you bristle – and I realise we haven’t even met – would you answer it if someone convinced you that your candour might just change the world? In her deliciously original first book, the former Guardian data journalist and illustrator Mona Chalabi sets out to do precisely that. The result – a dazzling mix of journalism, data visualisation and memoir – is both a joy to read and a serious provocation. Chalabi takes aim at our silence and furtiveness around individual income and finances. “Our collective ignorance is sustaining an unfair system,” she argues. Unless we talk more openly about our personal wealth, we will never be able to tackle the economic problems causing insecurity and anxiety for us all. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Man With Many Names by Georgi Gospodinov review – playful and profound tales from Bulgaria
articles.description: This collection of 40 short stories from the International Booker winner is full of invention and warmth In the titular story of Georgi Gospodinov’s short-story collection The Man With Many Names, the narrator reveals: “Telling our personal stories is the only move we can make … that allows us to postpone for at least a little while this game’s foregone ending.” It’s as good a description as any of the Bulgarian author’s preoccupation with stories and their power to upset life’s linear course. Like his idol Jorge Luis Borges, Gospodinov tends towards subversion in his fiction: he takes the “game” and rewrites the rules, turns the board upside down to find new ways of looking and seeing. If the ending is a foregone conclusion, Gospodinov’s magic is to make his stories feel like beginnings with endless possibilities. The Man With Many Names comprises 40 stories made up of two collections previously published in Bulgarian. Ranging from post-Communist realism to experimental fables set in unfamiliar worlds, these magnificently imaginative pieces trade in many of the same themes – childhood, the labyrinthine qualities of language, the push and pull of fantasy and reality – as his best-k

Universal basic income, autonomous vehicles and constant surveillance steering citizens towards their best lives are welcomed by most Icelanders, where only a few dissidents insist on living off-grid. When one of them is found murdered in a way that should have been impossible, questions are raised about the supposedly perfect system, creating fractures in the victim’s family – one of whom helped to establish the ruling AI, and still works closely with it. A fascinating, thoughtful, suspenseful tale grounded in believable characters, this could hardly be more timely. articles.title: How years of research built Grand Theft Auto VI’s obsessively detailed world
articles.description: The developers behind its virtual Florida share how they built their most ambitious world so far • Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here In 2015, a group of Grand Theft Auto developers from Rockstar North took their first trips to Miami to do field research for the next game in the phenomenally popular crime series. “Before you’re doing hyper-organised research trips, you’re immersing yourself in the place and its history, the vibe of it,” Rob Nelson, one of the lead developers on GTA VI, tells me. “[You see] the physical places you want to move characters through, the experiences you want them to have, and the juxtaposition between the extremes of society that are in Miami.” I wondered: did people ever recognise them on any of their research trips? Did locals know what they were doing? This is the biggest game in the world, after all; I imagine it would be difficult to go entirely undercover. “We’re always semi-undercover,” he says. “But if you have a bunch of dorks going through a terrifying neighbourhood, you do stick out a bit.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Crime pays: how Grand Theft Auto became a cultural colossus
articles.description: Ever since it crashed on to PC and consoles in the late 90s, GTA has been tearing up the game-making rulebook. We explore how its cultural references, rebel spirit and sprawling sense of freedom make it a definitive work of art In the 00s, when the Grand Theft Auto developer Rockstar Games revealed a new project, video game writers from all over the UK would make the journey to the company’s office in London. They would be ushered one by one into a darkened room to sit facing an enormous TV. There would be a dish of sweets on a low bench in front of them but, in the reverential hush that descended, it was never entirely clear if it was acceptable to eat them. After a few moments, the screen would come to life. Rockstar would sometimes begin its presentation not with footage from its new game, but clips from classic movies. This is the context of what we are making, Rockstar was saying, and that is where we belong. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has revived the midnight game launch – but was it worth the wait?
articles.description: When our writer found himself among the hundreds on Oxford Street hoping to get their hands on early copies and collectibles, it was a heartwarming reminder of the shared experience of fandom • The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time review – a dream come true It is Thursday night and I am sat blurry-eyed and runny nosed outside the Argos on Oxford Street. Incredibly, I am far from alone. This is not some strange protest against the popular retailer. When the clock strikes midnight, the lavish 4K Switch 2 remake of beloved N64 classic The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time will be released, and I have joined a lengthy queue of about 500 fans desperate to snag early copies. There are similar events taking place across the world, from Melbourne to Mexico City; at key locations, Nintendo has senior executives waiting at the tills. These days, of course, most video games are bought as digital copies that download straight to your PC or console on the day of release. You don’t even have to get out of bed to start playing. But in a bygone era, when we used to go to shops to buy games, midnight launches offered a space for likeminded enthusiasts to gather and celebrate their fandom. Every Call

articles.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time review – a dream come true
articles.description: Nintendo Switch 2; Nintendo This ambitious remake transforms a landmark Zelda game into a modern masterpiece, clearer and easier to navigate, more beautiful to look at, with playful musical touches. Yet the melancholy remains It’s always a worry, returning to a formative piece of art from your childhood. Will your jaded adult sensibilities render you unable to locate the magic that captivated your child self? Will revisiting it reveal that it was never actually that good, and that your tastes are built on a foundation of lies? With video games, there is the added complication of technological advancement: decades-old games can look so basic and feel so treacly to play that it’s hard to explain why they were mind-blowing at the time. Light-touch remasters aim to bring such games up to modern graphical standards without fundamentally changing them; an ambitious remake attempts to transform the work into something that can stand alongside any modern masterpiece. Ocarina of Time is the latter. And I could not be more delighted to report that it is a dream come true. Continue reading...

articles.title: Caryl Churchill’s magnificent Cloud 9 reaches for the skies – the National Theatre has done it proud
articles.description: National Theatre, London The experimental 1979 drama gleefully muddles roles in a century-spanning caper that bounces from colonial Africa to hippy London Caryl Churchill’s time-hopping 1979 drama is not revived as often as it might be, perhaps because it is so magnificently madcap. Bouncing from a first act satirising Victorian life in colonial Africa to a second act exploring sexual liberation in 1970s London, it could easily roll off-kilter in the wrong hands. There is also its complicated framework. Cloud 9 is a play in two distinct parts which follows some of the characters a century on, although they only age 25 years in that time and are played by different actors through ironic cross-casting. Thankfully this crisp, handsome and note-perfect revival lands in exactly the right hands with director Dominic Cooke, clear as crystal despite the complications, sizzling with satire but showing itself to be a deadly serious, and still highly topical, play about identity beneath its playful sending up of everything from empire and Britishness to the confinements of marriage. Continue reading...

articles.title: Old Vic 2027 season to feature Damian Lewis in a ‘provocative’ Henry V and Milly Alcock as Miss Julie
articles.description: Rupert Goold begins his tenure as artistic director with a version of Shakespeare’s history play, followed by shows starring Supergirl’s Alcock and Arinzé Kene Damian Lewis is to play Henry V at the Old Vic in London in the first production under the theatre’s new artistic director, Rupert Goold. Goold will direct what is billed as a “provocative” version of Shakespeare’s history play that challenges “what makes a leader a legend”. It will be Lewis’s first major theatre role since he starred in The Goat, or Who Is Sylvia? almost 10 years ago. He has previously played Romeo and Hamlet on stage, as well as appearing in Cymbeline and Much Ado About Nothing for the Royal Shakespeare Company. Continue reading...

articles.title: There’s scurvy, mutiny and mystery in Dogstar – but like its icebound ship this drama goes nowhere
articles.description: Hampstead theatre, London A bickering trio of trapped survivors who have lost their comrades are kept in an ominous stasis in Daisy Bell’s play The setup is strong in Daisy Hall’s follow-up to her debut, Bellringers . A few survivors on a whaling ship trapped in arctic ice are figuring out how to break free as the ice groans and explodes ominously around them. Babben (Justin Edwards) is an old hand who has whaled for almost 40 years; Gorey (Adam Rojko Vega) is a mischief-maker who walks around with a gun; the youngest, and most strait-laced, is Sam (Abdul Jalloh) who seems immobilised by anxiety. Continue reading...

articles.title: Orbiting Orbital review – Nitin Sawhney casts a spell inspired by Samantha Harvey’s Booker winner
articles.description: Schwarzman Centre, Oxford Nitin Sawhney’s eclectic global fusion brings in new writings from Harvey, drawings by Antony Gormley and collaborations from academics in space and ecosystems Samantha Harvey’s Booker-winning novel Orbital ends in music – an ecstatic word-orchestra of sound summoning not the music of the spheres, but Earth itself: “the rin-tin-tin and jumbled tumbling of static galactic woodwind rainforest trance of a wild and lilting world”. It’s a brave person who’d try to turn those imagined sounds into soundtrack; enter Nitin Sawhney – multi-award-winning musician, composer and producer – and a team of seriously starry friends. Commissioned by Oxford University’s Schwarzman Centre, Orbiting Orbital is a bewilderingly broad project that brings together six new pieces of writing by Harvey, music (old and newly composed) by Sawhney, drawings by Antony Gormley, photographs by Mary McCartney, as well as collaborations with academic in fields as disparate as space instrumentation and ecosystem science. articles.title: The space rocket I could have been aboard explodes: Rhiannon Adam’s best photograph
articles.description: ‘I was chosen to go around the Moon on a SpaceX starship. Preparations took over my life. Then, four minutes into watching a rocket on a test flight, it broke apart. And that was the end of my adventure’ This photograph was taken on 20 April 2023 from the VIP section of SpaceX’s launch viewing area, looking out from South Padre Island, Texas, towards Boca Chica, a nature reserve near the Mexican border which is home to SpaceX’s Starbase launchpad. In 2021, I and seven other civilians were selected from an open call to go around the Moon on a free SpaceX Starship flight funded by the Japanese billionaire Yusaku Maezawa. The dearMoon Project included myself and another photographer. For me, the story also became about being plucked from obscurity and planted in this very surreal world I could never have imagined being a part of in a million years. At the time, only 24 white American men had orbited or landed on the moon. Being selected for something like that changes your life and your perception of your worth in the world. articles.title: Jilly Cooper’s beloved typewriter could fetch £8,000 at auction
articles.description: Trusty Olivetti machine named ‘Monica 2’ was used for writer’s racy Rutshire chronicles One of Jilly Cooper’s beloved manual typewriters – used to write her bestselling, scandal-filled Rutshire chronicles – is to go under the hammer at auction. The Olivetti Underwood Lettera 32, which has a guide price of £5,000 to £8,000, was affectionately known by the late author as Monica 2. Continue reading...

articles.title: Stacy Keach obituary
articles.description: Versatile American stage and screen actor whose roles ranged from Hamlet to the tough private eye Mike Hammer There have been few actors as inexhaustible as Stacy Keach, who has died aged 85. Throughout a long career that began in his childhood he was equally active in theatre, films and TV, moving from the sublime to the ridiculous and back again with aplomb. Perhaps it was his ubiquity and eclecticism that caused him to be so underrated. Keach meant different things to different people. To theatregoers, he was a fine Shakespearean actor, acclaimed for his Hamlet, who was also adept in other classics and musicals (Barnum, Camelot, The King and I). To the filmgoer, he was one of the faces of Hollywood in the 1970s. To the television viewer, Keach was the tough private eye Mike Hammer, in the 80s TV series and spinoffs based on the novels by Mickey Spillane. Continue reading...

articles.title: BBCSO/Oramo review – yes, Inmo Yang is phenomenal but the BBC Symphony shone even brighter tonight
articles.description: Barbican Hall, London There was poise and passion in the Korean violinist’s Bartók, with Sakari Oramo and the BBC Symphony adding bite and touches of humour In a classical music world where virtuosity comes as standard, only a handful of soloists find themselves regularly described as a “phenomenon”. Korean violinist Inmo Yang is among them – and he’s still on the rise, more than a decade after his first major competition win and three years since making his UK debut with the BBC Symphony Orchestra and their chief conductor Sakari Oramo . Reunited here with the same musicians for Bartók’s early Violin Concerto No 1, Yang was all poise and passion, delivering the long, winding paragraph for the soloist that opens the work with characteristically supple elegance. His tone was tender – almost retro, in fact, in its natty sweetness – even in the more energetic portions of the second movement. This was a performance drawn throughout in a lyrical cursive: lovely, but monochromatically earnest. articles.title: The 37 best Christmas gifts in the UK for tweens – chosen by 10- to 12-year-olds
articles.description: We asked 20 tweenagers what they already own, love and think would make great gifts. Turns out it’s Lego, dance mats and plenty of lotions and potions • The best Christmas gifts for teenagers Buying for someone in the tweenage years can be a balancing act: while some kids are still crafting, enjoying board games and deep into Lego, others have moved on to skincare and guitars. So, in an effort to cover the whole range, I spoke to 20 tweens (from 10 to 12 years old) from across the country. But instead of asking what they want, I quizzed them on the things they already have, truly love and use regularly. Here are their tried and tested gift ideas for a range of prices. Continue reading...

articles.title: How I Christmas Shop with Jamie Oliver: ‘The most important thing? Gravy.’
articles.description: Always wondered how celebrities do Christmas, what they wear, eat, and always buy ready-made? The chef and campaigner talks whisky, matching waistcoats and the joy of a local bookshop with the Filter • Don’t get the Filter delivered to your inbox? articles.title: Are walking pads worth it? We put the best under-desk treadmills to the test
articles.description: Want to get your steps in while working or watching TV? Our expert puts walking pads through their paces to find the best for comfort, noise and ease of storage • The best treadmills for your home You don’t necessarily need to walk 10,000 steps a day to improve your health and wellbeing. In fact, the NHS encourages a slightly more manageable target of just 10 minutes of brisk walking daily to introduce more moderate-intensity physical activity and reduce your risk of early death by up to 15% . However, even squeezing in “brisk walks” can be a chore, with busy schedules and increasingly desk-bound jobs forcing more of us to remain sedentary for long periods. That is where walking pads come in, being lighter, smaller and often easier to store than bulky and tricky-to-manoeuvre running treadmills. Continue reading...

articles.title: The best Christmas things aren’t new – and that’s precisely the point
articles.description: Whether it’s vintage baubles or homemade gifts, there’s joy in a Christmas full of memories and personal touches. Plus, the best coats to keep out the chill this winter • Don’t get the Filter delivered to your inbox? Sign up here What’s the Christmas decoration you’ve had the longest? Mine is a set of silver paper streamers that originally belonged to my grandparents (and which, if the price in shillings on the original box is anything to go by, pre-date 1971). When I get them out, I can picture my late dad balanced on a chair, pinning them to my childhood dining room ceiling. It’s the old, slightly broken stuff that makes Christmas: the things you bring out every year, imbued with Christmases past. “I love finding a prime spot on the tree for a little beaded fairy I got at a fair in primary school,” says Filter audience editor Ella Jinadu. “It has pipe cleaner arms and legs so you can wrap it around the tree in different poses. articles.title: The best men’s coats for autumn and winter: 48 favourites for £200 or less
articles.description: From a puffer made of old fishing nets to a trench worthy of Bogart, these are the coats worth braving the cold for • The best men’s shirts for every occasion No one remembers the suit Humphrey Bogart wore at the end of Casablanca, but everyone remembers the trench. The same goes for you this winter: from November to March, your coat is your first impression, so it’s worth getting right. That doesn’t mean you have to spend a fortune: the coats in this list cost £200 or less. The trick to choosing the best coat for you is buying something you’ll still be happy to wear in five years. If you’re feeling unsure, stick to timeless colours – navy, black, camel, brown or moody greens – and shapes that have been around forever: the overcoat, the trench, the car coat or, a more recent classic, the puffer. And when uncertain about fit, always size up – outerwear looks best worn a little loose, and it leaves room for knitwear when freezing January rolls around. Continue reading...

articles.title: Jess Cartner-Morley on fashion: this season’s big idea? Wear a skirt. It’s that simple
articles.description: All you need to look on-trend this autumn is a skirt, but instead of going shopping, check what you already have in your wardrobe I go to a lot of fashion shows, and sometimes they are gorgeous and sometimes they are ugly. Sometimes they are electrifying and sometimes they are deathly dull. Sometimes they are completely baffling. My absolute favourite kind of show is the one that makes me want to run home and change my outfit. A show that makes me think: there it is! That’s exactly what I want to wear. When the look speaks to me, as if it had been on the tip of my tongue. God, I love that. Which is what happened at Prada this season . The idea was: skirts. That’s it, that’s the whole idea. The show was 63 different skirts – some with a sweater, some with a bra top, some with a jacket, but the point was the skirts. They were knee-length, give or take an inch up or down, and A-line, although sometimes a narrow almost-pencil and other times with a broader flare. There were skirts that wrapped like kilts, held together with strips of industrial-weight Velcro embroidered with tiny gems. articles.title: Touch of evil: the terrifying truth about sleep paralysis
articles.description: One in five people have experienced this frightening state – and the Harvard neuroscientist Baland Jalal has dedicated his career to studying it. Could it be a portal to a deeper understanding of the mind? The Harvard neuroscientist Baland Jalal is considering the unfathomable depths of the human brain. “It can contemplate itself, and vast galaxies, spirits, souls, poetry, Einstein. Yet you hold it in your hand and it seems so trivial.” Jalal’s passion – the subject that drove him to become a scientist – is sleep paralysis, a brain glitch that can fill its host with terror so palpable that it can cause lasting trauma. “What you get very close to in sleep paralysis,” he says, “is that subjective world of the mind. It’s very hard to put into words.” He should know – he’s spent 271 pages trying to do so. His new book, The Phantom Mind, argues that by exploring the borderlands of sleep, where sleep paralysis occurs, we can delve deeper into how all aspects of our minds work. articles.title: ‘How do we get out of our midweek menu rut’? – Feast’s Rukmini Iyer answered your cooking questions
articles.description: Rukmini Iyer, author of the bestselling cookbook series Roasting Tin, answered your queries from ideas for simple weeknight meals that can be prepped in 15 minutes to leftovers for lunches and whether one pan is always better than two Ask a question: log in or sign up here Swinehead asks : Is it better not to use baking paper (even though it is easier to clean up afterwards) so as to get a better “roasting” of ingredients? In the oven, if you’ve found baking paper makes things steamier, then I’d not use it.
